newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Nations favor new world court, split over power.
newsitem.headline: Nations favor new world court, split over power.

text.p: U.N. members all say they favor setting up the world's first permanent international criminal court but some of their proposals would virtually kill its ability to function.

"The momentum for an international criminal court is irreversible," said Richard Dicker of the New York-based Human Rights Watch. "The question, however, is whether the court will be an effective body or a judicial Potemkin village."
Governments are fairly certain there will be a court to judge perpetrators of the world's most terrible crimes of genocide and massacres, a goal that has eluded the United Nations for half a century.

"I do not know of any member of the United Nations who is opposing its establishment," said Adriann Bos, the Dutch chairman of a U.N. committee that ended a two-week negotiation session on the court on Friday.
But critics fear that too much involvement by national governments as well as the 15-member U.N. Security Council would politicize the court and tarnish its independence.

The proposed new court is separate from the International Court of Justice at The Hague, which deals with disputes between nations. Instead it is meant to build on the four ad hoc tribunals that have prosecuted heinous crimes since 1945.

The first tribunals to try war criminals were created in Nuremberg and Tokyo after the Second World War by the victorious allies. The Security Council in 1993 created a tribunal in The Hauge during the Yugoslav civil war and another one in Arusha, Tanzania after the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.
A high-level five-week conference is planned for Rome next year after legal experts from more than 100 countries attempt to reconcile a myriad of conflicting views.

At last week's session legal experts agreed on criteria in determining when a national court was unable or unwilling to prosecute an offender. But positions differed widely on who could bring a complaint to the new international court.

Some countries, including several in Europe and Latin America, would give a prosecutor the power to initiate cases while others, led by India and China, believe governments must request and consent to investigations.

And the five permanent Security Council members with veto power -- the United States, France, Britain, and China -- want a major role for the council, such as blocking any case from going to the court if it is before the 15-member body.

The United States and France have taken the toughest positions while China, Russia and Britain, whose new Labor government changed direction and declared itself in favor of the court, are said to be more open to compromises.
Critics say this will hobble the work of the prosecutors and leave the court open to political pressures.
"Such interference will be a body blow to the independence and impartiality of the court," Dicker said.
The United States backs the proposed court that will need to be established by an international treaty and probably will not be set up until after 2000.

But it insists on a key role for the Security Council and that the issues before the court be limited to genocide, crimes against humanity and serious war crimes, with strong references to sexual assault in each category.
Germany is pushing to have the crime of aggression included and India wants terrorism added to the list.

"You cannot have a system that tries to end-run the Security Council," said David Scheffer, the new U.S. ambassador for war crimes issues. He emphasized that the United States had to protect itself from frivolous complaints.
"There is a reality, and that reality is that the United States is a global military power and presence. Other countries are not. We are," he told reporters.

"Our military forces are often called upon to engage overseas in conflict situations, for purposes of humanitarian intervention, to rescue hostages, to bring out American citizens, to deal with terrorists," he added.
"We have to be extremely careful that this proposal does not limit the capacity of our armed forces to legitimately operate internationally," he said.
